extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychoanalysis, literary criticism, and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting psychoanalytic criteria for when and why things are comic or humorous, including conditions, mechanisms (discharge, displacement), infantile determinants, and formal devices (repetition, exaggeration, imitation, unmasking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic pleasure derives from a comparison of two expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic pleasure and its effect (laughter) can originate only when a difference resulting from a comparison of two expenditures is no longer utilizable and is capable of discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential diagnostic: identify a perceived difference between the expenditure (effort/energy) of the self and the other (or between two modes) that cannot be put to other use and therefore is discharged as comic pleasure. Anti-pattern: if the difference can be utilized productively, comic pleasure will not arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of Isolation of the Comic
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic often requires 'isolation' of the comic case — the comparison must be free from competing associations or uses that would divert the surplus energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce comic effect, the situation must be insulated so the surplus energy discharges as laughter; when associations, duties, or alternative utilizations intervene, the comic is lost. Example: conscious focus on the comparison (examiner comparing to standard) prevents comic discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favorable disposition: 'one is in the mood for laughing'
rubrics_metrics.description: A general happy disposition or euphoria makes almost everything seem comic because comparisons are measured against normal conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set mood/expectation to increase comic reception (audience intending to laugh at a farce will find slight differences comic). Conversely, lack of this disposition reduces incidental comic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation/premeditation enhances comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting oneself in the right mood or expecting comic material lowers the threshold: differences that would otherwise be overlooked can produce laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical: framing, signaling, or priming an audience increases laughter (theatre, comic lecture). Caution: performers share intention; one may later feel ashamed for laughing at premeditated comic content outside ordinary life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfavorable condition: serious mental activity blocks comic discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement in imaginative or serious mental activity disturbs the automatic discharge necessary for comic pleasure, requiring larger or unexpected differences to trigger laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid asking an audience already absorbed in abstract/serious thought to appreciate subtle comic discrepancies; interruptions of abstract contemplation can allow comic effects to break through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to the comparison destroys the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: If attention is fixed on the comparison that produces the comic, the comic force is lost; the comic process must proceed unnoticed (automatic/foreconscious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic delivery should avoid making the audience analytically compare at the time of the event. Example: an examiner perceives student nonsense as annoyance rather than comic; classmates laugh because they are not fixated on comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disturbing effect of strong affective release
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporaneous marked release of affect (painful or intense emotions) disturbs comic discharge and usually excludes comic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic material should avoid being presented in contexts where the audience is experiencing strong pain, pity, or anger; exceptions occur (e.g., 'bitter laughter') when magnitude or specific configuration allows comic discharge despite affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact-effect / pleasurable addition promotes comic discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Any additional pleasurable element accompanying a case can act like a contact-effect (fore-pleasure) and promote comic pleasure by aiding discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of incidental pleasurable stimuli can prime or magnify comic reception. Example: theatrical anticipation, shared convivial context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual/obscene comedic mechanism: exposure and omitted expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidental exposure produces comic effect because the spectator compares the ease of enjoyment with the great expenditure otherwise necessary; expositional contexts make the exposed person comical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic effect depends on third-person perspective and the omission of the effort needed for concealment; the spy who exerts effort loses comic effect (becomes sexual, not comic). Use unmasking/degradation carefully as they rely on perceived omitted expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infantile determination (relation to the child)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is closely related to the infantile: the comic often arises from perceiving the other (or oneself) as childlike, recalling 'lost infantile laughing' and differences between grown-up and childlike behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic techniques that evoke childishness (naiveté, lack of inhibition, motion-impulse, want of moderation) are effective. Note: children themselves often lack the comic feeling because they lack the comparative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three loci of comic comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic difference can arise (a) between the other and oneself (other appears childlike), (b) entirely within the other (the other puts himself on the child's level), or (c) entirely within oneself (one discovers the child in oneself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify comic devices by locus: (a) movement/forms/character (b) situation/exaggeration/imitation/degradation/unmasking (c) comic expectation/self-revelation. This helps choose which technique to apply for desired comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic situation: embarrassment and helplessness
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic situation is largely based on embarrassment, repetitions, and the helplessness reminiscent of the child's condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embarrassment, repeated mishaps, or helplessness are reliable sources of comic effect when isolated from strong affective involvement. Repetition (monotony) can be exploited for increasing comic effect (e.g., Mark Twain's recurring cow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration and caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration affords pleasure by echoing the child's want of moderation and ignorance of quantitative relations; when justified by reason, it pleases grown-ups as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measured exaggeration to mimic childlike excess; beware of overreach that provokes disbelief or hostility rather than laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is rooted in the child's best art and yields comic pleasure by reducing adults to a level that the child aspires to (imitating the 'big fellows').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic imitation should capture salient adult traits in a childlike or simplified form. Effective when the imitator's ambition to be 'big' is revealed as ludicrous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation and unmasking
rubrics_metrics.description: Degradation (lowering the grown-up to child's level) and unmasking produce comic pleasure by exposing dependence on physical needs or hypocrisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unmasking to reveal a mismatch between a character's presented ideal and their base impulses. Works well with satire and social comedy; ensure isolation so pity/anger won't override laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of expectation (anticipatory disappointment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic expectation depends on gullibility and anticipatory dispositions; grown-ups may experience comic disappointment as a source of laughter (this is developmentally late).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up expectations and then subvert them in a way that creates a harmless disappointment; be mindful that children may experience such cases as mere disappointment rather than comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as economy in expenditure of affect
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is characterised by economizing and redirecting affective energy: it allows pleasure despite painful affects by preventing their full release and transforming the held energy into humoristic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques: displace or deflect sympathy/anger/pity into a humorous framing; humor can be self-sufficient (one-person process) and may function as a defense mechanism that 'denies' painful affects their usual discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humoristic displacement (defense-process mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor functions like an elevated defense: it withdraws ideas connected with painful affect from conscious attention and changes the potential discharge into pleasure by displacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To craft humor in painful contexts, use displacement (redirect the energy to a secondary, comic element). Constraint: displacement must remain automatic/foreconscious; conscious analytic attention defeats it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of humor determined by the economized affect
rubrics_metrics.description: The varieties of humor depend on which emotional feeling is economized (sympathy, anger, pain, compassion, fear, disgust, etc.), and whether humor is fused with wit or other comic forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the target affect to economize and choose techniques accordingly (grim-humor for fear/disgust, satirical framing for anger). 'Broken' humor (smiling under tears) results from partial rather than total economizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic/foreconscious localization of comic and humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Both comic and humor operate in the foreconscious/automatic processes and require avoidance of conscious analytic attention; wit more directly engages unconscious–foreconscious compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comic elements to operate beneath explicit analysis (timing, implicit comparisons); do not prompt the audience to consciously reason through the comparison at the moment of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic requires dual modes of idea-application (basis for comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: A condition for the origin of the comic is applying to the same thought function two different modes of ideas (e.g., usual vs emergency expenditure, anticipated vs occurred), whose juxtaposition yields the comic difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create parallel or successive modes (schemas) for the audience to implicitly compare; juxtaposition of incongruent modes is a primary structural device for comedy. Example distinctions: stranger vs self, usual vs emergency, anticipated vs already occurred.
